column6: F: Every month, the same job. Opening balance, what moved, closing balance... | M: Fixed by hand, in a spreadsheet.

column5: The template is an Excel workbook.
column6: F: So what are we looking at? | M: An ordinary Excel workbook. Five sheets. This is your layout, and the tags say where each number goes. | F: How does it know what to read? | M: Seven short lines on the Process sheet. And BACKUP is the master copy.
F: Now, inside the ERP. | M: GardenWorld, the demo company. We log in as its admin.

column5: Excel Report, then the sample template.
column6: M: This pill is Excel Report. | F: And the sample template? | M: Right here.

column5: One January to thirty-first December, two thousand three.
column6: M: The whole of two thousand three.
F: Run! | M: Three queries. Forty-three milliseconds.
F: Look, it added the rows! | M: Twenty-one accounts, one row each. The totals moved down to row twenty-eight.
M: Debit, forty thousand, three hundred ninety-two, forty-four. Credit, exactly the same. | F: So it balances. | M: The difference is zero.

column5: One rule: edit BACKUP, never Output.
column6: M: One rule. Never type into Output. | F: Why not? | M: It is rebuilt from BACKUP on every run. Make your edits in BACKUP.

column5: Excel file and a one-page PDF.
column6: F: And what do I get out? | M: The Excel file, and a one-page PDF. | F: Is everything in it? | M: All twenty-one account codes, checked. The Thai text comes through intact.

column5: Free open-source code. No PDF subscription.
column6: F: Is there a PDF subscription to pay? | M: No. Free, open-source code, end to end. On our reference sheets, ninety-eight point six percent matches a commercial converter.

column5: You design it in Excel. We fill it in.
column6: F: So I keep my own design? | M: Exactly. You design it in Excel. We fill it in.
